Where it began

Anil Kumble was born in Bangalore on 17 October 1970. He grew up watching the great India spinner B. S. Chandrasekhar, learned the game on the streets of the city and was a member of the Young Cricketers club by the age of 13. Alongside the cricket he studied mechanical engineering, graduating in 1991–92.

He began as a fast bowler, and that never quite left him. When he first played for Karnataka, against Hyderabad in November 1989, the match brought him four wickets and a king pair, which is about as mixed a start as cricket allows.

The player

His first Test came at Manchester in 1990. He made the side his own on the 1992 tour of South Africa, and from then until 2008 he was at the heart of India's bowling. In 132 Tests from 1990 to 2008 he took 619 wickets at 29.65, with 35 five-wicket innings and eight ten-wicket matches. When he retired in 2008, only two bowlers in Test history had taken more.

The day everyone remembers is in Delhi in February 1999, when he took all ten Pakistan wickets for 74 runs, matching Jim Laker. In January 2008 at Perth he became the first Indian to reach 600 Test wickets, and he led India in 14 Tests near the end of his career.

What made him special

He never spun the ball very far. Instead he relied on pace, bounce, accuracy and a famous flipper, and he would bowl all day if asked, once sending down 72 overs in an innings. He was also a fine catcher of his own bowling: his 35 caught-and-bowled Test wickets were a world record.

Batting took him longer to master. His first Test hundred, 110 not out at the Oval against England in 2007, came in his 117th Test, the longest anyone had waited. He was the only man to take all ten wickets in an innings and make a Test hundred, so the wait was worth it.

Away from the middle

His speed through the air earned him the nickname Jumbo, after the jumbo jet. He was the leading wicket-taker at the 1996 World Cup, a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1996 and a winner of the Arjuna award and the Padma Shri. He entered the ICC Hall of Fame in 2015. Later he coached India from 2016 to 2017, chaired the ICC cricket committee and was President of the Karnataka State Cricket Association.

And finally

After his ten wickets in Delhi, a traffic circle in Bengaluru was named after him and he was given a car with the number plate KA-10-N-10. Not many bowlers can find their best figures on the road.
